title: Medically evacuated to Japan
description: Larry was medically evacuated from Vietnam to Japan — sick with what he called "sepititis" [likely hepatitis], malaria, and infections, having lost a great deal of weight. He described his stool as pure white and his urine like Coca-Cola, the classic signs of hepatitis jaundice. This answers the puzzle of his DD-214, which lists his last duty assignment as a U.S. Army medical command at APO San Francisco 96343 under U.S. Army Japan (USARJ): he finished his service in Japan as a patient, not on reassignment. He remembers arriving in early September and the weather turning cold, going into winter. From the hospital he befriended the man in the bed across from him, a fellow patient from back east; the two explored Tokyo together, including a basement German restaurant called "Heidelberg" off the Ginza — the likely story behind the cool-season Tokyo photographs. On 2026-08-13 Larry named the hospital himself, unprompted: "I was at Camp Zama in Japan in Sugami Uro" [Sagami-Ōno].
larrysRecollection: He went to Japan because he was sick — "sepititis" [as noted], malaria, and infections — and lost a bunch of weight. His stool was pure white and his urine looked like Coca-Cola. It was cold, going into winter; he placed it as early September.
researchNotes: The medical command on the DD-214 is documentary; the medevac-as-patient explanation is Larry's own account (2026-08-12 phone call, research/interviews/2026-08-12-call-notes.md) and fits the form's box 27 reading NONE for combat wounds. Larry independently confirmed the hospital on 2026-08-13 — told only that research had a high-confidence name, not what it was, he wrote "Camp Zama ... in Sugami Uro" [Sagami-Ōno] (data/recollections/giscus-stories-c18006833.json). That matches the documentary case for the U.S. Army Medical Center, Japan at Sagami-Ōno / Camp Zama (research/places/japan-hospital-1965.md): official AMEDD histories show it was effectively the only Army hospital in Japan receiving Vietnam evacuees before December 1965 — the 249th General (Camp Drake) and 106th General (Kishine) both opened that December, after he was home — and it admitted 462 Vietnam malaria patients in August–December 1965. APO 96343 is Camp Zama's. Confirmation route: NPRC clinical records, filed by hospital name. "Early September" and "cold, going into winter" don't fit together in Tokyo, but a September arrival with the stay running toward his November 30 separation covers both.
